title: Apple Computer, maker of the Apple II, goes public
what: Apple Computer went public on 12 December: 4.6 million shares at 22 dollars raised over 100 million dollars, the biggest offering since Ford in 1956, and by the close they traded at 29. It makes the Apple II, a small computer for homes, schools and offices; sales were 118 million dollars in its last financial year. The founders, Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, and about 300 others became millionaires.
why: The listing beat. Apple was the leader of the young personal computer market; nobody yet knew that IBM would enter it eight months later.

title: Apple lays off staff over the troubled Apple III; Jobs becomes chairman
what: The Apple III, the office computer launched in November at 4,340 dollars and more, has been plagued by faults: machines overheat and fail. President Mike Scott laid off employees in February to cut costs, a move co-founder Steve Jobs opposed. Mike Markkula takes over as president and Jobs becomes chairman. The shares, 22 dollars at the December float, have been falling since January.
why: The first crisis of the listed Apple: the Apple III failure (Wozniak later said it had "100 percent hardware failures") and the first management shake-up. Sets up the 1981 slide.
changed: note to the writer addressed: the Boeing 767 has a story of its own in September 1982, when it entered service with United

title: Apple shares drop 21% from their May high
what: Apple shares fell 21% in June, giving back the rise of April and May, in a flat market. Investors have little to go on beyond the Apple III's reliability problems and talk that IBM, the giant of the computer industry, is preparing its own personal computer. Apple is still growing fast on the Apple II, but the stock market is no longer sure what a young computer company should be worth.
why: No specific June event found (searched UPI, Wikipedia, company histories); the fall follows a 36% rise in April-May and precedes the IBM PC of 12 August, so this reads as the end of the post-IPO enthusiasm against the Apple III background. The IBM rumour is contextual: the PC was announced two months later; the beat says "talk", not a sourced report. Curator asked about this month.
source: price changes from data/out/aapl.json and data/reference/sp500.json; context https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_III (read 2026-10-03)

title: Apple replaces the first 14,000 Apple IIIs with a redesigned model
what: Apple is replacing the first 14,000 Apple III computers it sold with a redesigned version that fixes the overheating and faulty circuit boards of the original. The machine, launched a year ago as Apple's step into the office, has sold poorly against the Apple II that still carries the company.
why: Closes the Apple III chapter for 1981; the product never recovered. December +19% is not tied to this.

title: Falling interest rates power a second leap
what: By October inflation had fallen to about 5% and long-term interest rates were coming down as the Federal Reserve let its key rate fall back to about 9%. The stock market rose another 11% in October. Apple, the best-known maker of personal computers, is one of the most popular growth stocks. The numbers: the Fed's rate 9.7 percent. Inflation 4.9 percent. Unemployment 10.1 percent.
why: Same rally as August, with Apple again rising three times as much as the market.
source: https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/recession-of-1981-82 (read 2026-10-03); data/reference/sp500.json and data/out/aapl.json (monthly prices); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS, CPIAUCSL and UNRATE (downloaded 2026-10-04)
changed: note to the writer addressed: joined the interest-rate storyline, with the three numbers and the chart

title: Apple unveils the Lisa
what: Apple introduced the Lisa computer on 19 January. It is controlled with a mouse and pictures on the screen instead of typed commands and costs 9,995 dollars with a hard disk. Apple spent heavily to develop it and is betting it will win over business users.
why: The shares rose 37% in the month on the launch and the market boom. The Lisa itself flopped: perhaps 10,000 to 60,000 sold and a large loss; its ideas lived on in the Macintosh.

title: Apple shares lose more than a third in a month
what: Apple's shares, which stood at 63 dollars in June, have collapsed: in September alone they lost 38%. Computer shares fell across the board after Osborne, a maker of portable computers, went bankrupt. Apple has troubles of its own: its new Lisa costs 10,000 dollars and sells poorly, it has cut the price of its best seller, the Apple IIe, and IBM, only two years after launching its PC, now sells more personal computers by value than Apple.
why: The first Apple crash: the company that invented the market is being overtaken by IBM. It sets up the Macintosh of January 1984 as the answer.

title: The Macintosh
what: Apple presented the Macintosh on 24 January, two days after a 1.5 million dollar television commercial by the film director Ridley Scott ran during the Super Bowl. The Mac is worked with a mouse and pictures on the screen, has a 9-inch screen and 128 kilobytes of memory, and costs 2,495 dollars. The commercial, seen by some 43 million Americans, shows a young woman smashing the screen of a 'Big Brother' who stands for IBM.
why: The product that defined Apple's identity for a generation, though early sales disappointed.
changed: note to the writer addressed: link to the Super Bowl advert added (a new link field, shown under the story)

title: 'Apple II Forever': a portable Apple, and the shares jump 27 percent
what: Three months after the Macintosh, Apple showed on 24 April that it is not giving up the computer that made it big. At an event called 'Apple II Forever' it presented the Apple IIc, a small Apple II that weighs 3.4 kilograms, has the disk drive built in and can be carried from room to room. It costs 1,295 dollars, about half as much as a Macintosh, and Apple wants to sell 400,000 of them this year. The shares gained 27 percent in April.
why: The Apple II family still earned most of Apple's money in 1984; the Macintosh needed years to take over. The link between the launch and the jump in the shares is the likely one, not a documented one.
changed: new beat requested by the curator: explains Apple +27% in April 1984

title: Steve Jobs leaves Apple
what: On 17 September Steve Jobs, Apple's co-founder and chairman, resigned. In the spring the board had backed chief executive John Sculley, hired from PepsiCo in 1983, when he took the Macintosh division away from Jobs. Five senior employees are leaving with Jobs to start a new company, and Jobs has sold nearly all of his Apple shares.
why: The end of the founder era. Jobs's new company, NeXT, would bring him back to Apple eleven years later.

title: Apple pays its first dividend
what: On 11 May Apple declared its first dividend. The Macintosh Plus and the new Macintosh II with colour are selling well to businesses, designers and schools, and the Mac with Apple's LaserWriter printer has become the tool for desktop publishing.
why: Apple at the height of the Sculley years: profitable, growing, paying dividends. The shares nearly doubled in 1986 and doubled again in 1987. (Time check: removed the June share split from this May beat.)

title: Apple's first portable Macintosh
what: Apple released the Macintosh Portable on 20 September, its first battery-powered computer, at 5,799 dollars. The Mac line is selling well.
why: 1989 to 1991 were later called the first golden age of the Mac; the Portable itself failed, the PowerBook of 1991 succeeded. (Time check: cut the hindsight judgement 'these are good years for Apple'.)

title: Windows 3.0 gives PCs what made the Mac special
what: Microsoft launched Windows 3.0 on 22 May. It gives ordinary IBM-compatible PCs a screen with windows, icons and a mouse much like the Macintosh, at lower prices. Apple's Macs still sell well, but the PCs are catching up.
why: The long squeeze on Apple's margins and market share begins; 1989-91 was the 'first golden age' of the Mac. (Time check: dropped the foreshadowing 'for now'.)

title: Apple goes cheap: the Macintosh Classic for 999 dollars
what: On 15 October Apple presented the Macintosh Classic and the Macintosh LC, its first Macs priced for schools and homes: chairman John Sculley said prices would start at 1,000 dollars, less than half of what a Mac used to cost. Apple wants the Macintosh in many more hands. Investors are uneasy, because cheaper machines earn thinner profits on each sale.
why: The turn that leads into the 1991 collapse: volume up, margins down. The investor concern is stated in the source.

title: Apple shares fall 15%: cheap Macs sell, but the profit on each is thin
what: Apple shares fell 15% in May after a 19% fall in April. The low-priced Macintosh Classic and LC are selling, but Apple earns far less on each one, and the company said it would offset the lower gross margins by cutting operating expenses. Reports in mid-May spoke of 600 to 2,000 of the 15,600 jobs going, mostly in administration; Apple would not confirm a figure.
why: Two months into a three-month slide of 39% from the March peak. The margin problem and the layoff reports are from the Seattle Times of 18 May 1991; the share figures from the data. The April fall has no separate source and is folded in here.

title: Apple cuts about 1,500 jobs; shares down 39% since March
what: Apple announced the cuts investors had been waiting for: about 1,500 jobs, a tenth of its staff, to bring costs in line with the thinner profits of its cheaper Macintosh models. The shares fell another 12% in June and have lost 39% since March, in a month when the whole market fell 5%. Apple remains profitable; the question is how much it can earn selling computers at 1,000 dollars instead of 2,500.
why: Closes the 1991 slide. The 1,500 figure comes only from search-result summaries of later press (SFGate, Post-Bulletin) because the pages themselves would not load; the exact announcement date is not established. Curator asked for this story. The July 1991 IBM alliance is the next beat.
source: SFGate "Apple layoffs: Painful but necessary" and Post-Bulletin, via search summaries (pages did not load) (read 2026-10-03); Seattle Times 1991-05-18 for the staff total; price changes from data/out/aapl.json

title: Apple and IBM, enemies for a decade, agree to work together
what: On 3 July Apple and IBM signed a letter of intent for an alliance that would have been unthinkable a few years ago: a new family of microprocessors with Motorola, derived from IBM's POWER chips, a joint company to build a next-generation operating system from Apple's "Pink" project, and another for multimedia software. The aim is a common platform that other makers can build on, a direct challenge to the Microsoft-and-Intel world of the PC. Apple shares rose 11% in July.
why: The strategic answer to the margin squeeze and to Windows. The formal contract followed on 2 October 1991. Whether the rise was caused by the alliance is inferred from timing.

title: Apple replaces its chief executive as a price war eats its profit
what: On 18 June Apple's board replaced John Sculley as chief executive with Michael Spindler, until now the number two; Sculley stays on as chairman. A price war among PC makers is forcing Apple to sell its Macintosh computers ever more cheaply, and its profit is shrinking fast. The shares lost 30% in June.
why: Explains the fall of June 1993 and prepares the story of October, when Sculley leaves altogether. Apple earned 86 million dollars in fiscal 1993 after 530 million the year before.

title: Sculley leaves Apple for good; Spindler cuts jobs
what: John Sculley, replaced as chief executive in June, has now left Apple altogether after a bad year and a price war in personal computers; Michael Spindler runs the company and is cutting jobs, projects and research. Under Sculley sales grew from about 800 million to 7.9 billion dollars a year.
why: The start of the slide that brought Apple close to collapse by 1997. Sources differ on the date: Spindler is often said to have become CEO in June 1993; Wikipedia gives 15 October 1993, the date Sculley also left the board. The beat follows Wikipedia.

title: The Power Macintosh
what: Apple has started its Power Macintosh line, built on PowerPC processors developed in an alliance with IBM and Motorola. Parts of the Mac's software were rewritten so that older programs still run.
why: In 1995 Apple began licensing the Mac system to clone makers, whose machines took sales from Apple's own; Jobs ended the program in 1997. The exact launch month of the Power Mac is not in the sources read; the beat sits in spring 1994. (Time check: title mentioned Mac clones, which were not part of the news in March 1994.)

title: Gil Amelio replaces Spindler; Apple's survival in question
what: On 2 February Apple named Gil Amelio, head of National Semiconductor, as chief executive, replacing Michael Spindler. Apple could not build enough of its popular models and too many of the others, its finance chief left in 1995 after urging a sale of the company, and merger talks with IBM, Sun and Philips came to nothing. Fortune wrote this month that the company that invented the personal computer will likely disappear.
why: The near-death years: Amelio cut a third of the workforce, and the stock fell 81% from 1991 to December 1997.

title: Apple buys NeXT, and Jobs is back
what: On 20 December Apple announced it will buy NeXT, Steve Jobs's company, for 429 million dollars and 1.5 million Apple shares. NeXT's operating system will become the basis of the next Mac system, which Apple failed to build itself, and the deal brings Jobs back into Apple's management.
why: The most important deal in Apple's history; NeXT's software became the foundation of Mac OS X.

title: Jobs makes peace with Microsoft
what: Gil Amelio was pushed out as chief executive on 9 July, and Steve Jobs is now interim chief executive. At the Macworld show on 6 August Jobs announced that Microsoft will invest 150 million dollars in Apple, keep making Office for the Mac for five years and settle the long patent dispute. Apple is worth only about 2.5 billion dollars.
why: Mostly symbolic money (Apple had 1.2 billion in cash) but a vital signal that the Mac would survive; +24% in the month after +23% in July.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Apple_Inc. (read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/0000320193-97-000012.txt (Apple 8-K with press release of 9 July 1997) (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Amelio (read 2026-10-03)

title: Apple is profitable again
what: At the Macworld show on 6 January Apple announced that it expects a profit of more than 45 million dollars on sales of about 1.575 billion for the quarter to December, its first good news in years. Jobs has cut the product line, ended the licensing of the Mac to clone makers and opened an online store.
why: The turning point of the comeback; +40% in the month after an 81% fall from 1991 to December 1997.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/0000320193-98-000001.txt (Apple 8-K with press release of 6 January 1998, read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Apple_Inc. (read 2026-10-03)

title: Apple's sales warning halves the shares
what: At the end of September Apple warned that sales for the quarter to September will fall well short of its expectations. The new G4 Cube computer, launched in July, is selling far below plan, education sales are weak, and buyers chose cheaper Power Macs; dealers are sitting on unsold computers. Apple expects sales to fall sharply in the next quarter as well.
why: The -58% month ended the first comeback rally. The 10-K later put the shortfall at about 180 million dollars, half of it the Cube. The exact date of the warning is not in the sources read.

title: The iPod: a thousand songs in your pocket
what: Apple introduced the iPod, a portable music player with a 5-gigabyte hard disk that holds about 1,000 songs and works with Apple's iTunes software on the Mac. It is controlled with a scroll wheel and goes on sale on 10 November for 399 dollars, a lot for a music player.
why: The product that turned Apple from a computer maker into a consumer-electronics company; its effect on profits showed from 2004.

title: The iTunes Music Store opens
what: Apple opened the iTunes Music Store, where songs can be bought legally for download. For now it works only with Macs and in the United States.
why: Made the iPod a system; a Windows version followed in October 2003 and opened the iPod to the whole PC market. (Time check: cut the sales figure for the first 16 days, which ran into May.)

title: Two million iPods in a quarter
what: On 13 October Apple reported a profit of 106 million dollars on sales of 2.35 billion for the quarter to September, sales up 37%. It shipped 2,016,000 iPods, five times as many as a year earlier, its retail stores' sales grew 95%, and it expects a much better December quarter.
why: The moment investors understood the iPod effect; +35% in the month and the start of a tenfold rise to 2007.

title: Apple switches the Mac to Intel
what: On 6 June Steve Jobs announced that Apple will put Intel processors into its Macintosh computers from 2006, replacing the PowerPC chips from IBM and Motorola. Apple has secretly kept a version of Mac OS X running on Intel chips for five years. Paul Otellini, Intel's chief executive since 18 May, worked to win the deal.
why: The transition finished in 2006, a year ahead of the original plan.

title: Apple unveils the iPhone and drops 'Computer' from its name
what: On 9 January Steve Jobs presented the iPhone, a mobile phone, music player and internet device operated with the fingers on a touch screen, and Apple Computer renamed itself Apple Inc. The iPhone goes on sale in the United States in June.
why: The product that made Apple the most valuable company in the world.

title: Record results, weak forecast, falling market
what: On 22 January Apple reported its best quarter ever: revenue of 9.6 billion dollars, up 35%, and a profit of 1.58 billion, with 2.3 million iPhones sold. But it forecast revenue of only about 6.8 billion dollars for the next quarter, and stock markets are falling.
why: -32% in the month: a cautious forecast in a falling market after the shares had doubled in 2007.

title: Apple announces the iPad
what: On 27 January Apple announced the iPad, a tablet computer with a screen twice the size of the iPhone's, without phone functions. It goes on sale in April.
why: A new product category; Apple's third hit in a decade.

title: Jobs resigns; Tim Cook is chief executive
what: On 24 August Steve Jobs resigned as Apple's chief executive, writing to the board that he could no longer meet his duties and expectations. Tim Cook succeeds him.
why: The handover the market had feared went smoothly; the shares barely moved.

title: Steve Jobs dies
what: Steve Jobs died at his home in Palo Alto on 5 October, aged 56, after a relapse of the pancreatic tumour first diagnosed in 2003. He co-founded Apple, had stepped down as chief executive six weeks earlier, and was behind the Macintosh, the iPod, the iPhone and the iPad.
why: The end of an era; Apple's best years for shareholders were still to come.

title: A record stock market value
what: On 20 August Apple's rising shares made it worth a record 624 billion dollars, beating the record set by Microsoft in 1999 (without adjusting for inflation).
why: The peak before a 40% fall to June 2013.

title: A seven-for-one split and 130 billion dollars for shareholders
what: On 23 April Apple said it will return more than 130 billion dollars to shareholders by the end of 2015, raise its share buyback to 90 billion dollars and its dividend by about 8%, and split its shares seven for one. Apple has paid a dividend again since 2012, its first since 1995.
why: Cook's Apple as a cash machine; the shares recovered from the 2013 slump.

title: Apple's first sales decline in years
what: On 26 April Apple reported revenue of 50.6 billion dollars for the quarter to March, down from 58 billion a year earlier, as iPhone sales fell; Tim Cook pointed to strong growth in services and more than a billion active Apple devices. Apple raised its capital return program to 250 billion dollars. In March 2015 Apple joined the Dow Jones index and in April 2015 its Watch went on sale.
why: The worry that the iPhone had peaked; the answer was services sold to the installed base.

title: The iPhone X
what: On 12 September Apple introduced the iPhone X, with facial recognition and wireless charging, alongside the iPhone 8, at the new Steve Jobs Theater.
why: The tenth-anniversary iPhone.

title: The first trillion-dollar company
what: On 2 August Apple became the first US listed company to be worth one trillion dollars.
why: +20% in the month; the milestone of the iPhone era.

title: Tim Cook warns: China and fewer iPhone upgrades
what: On 2 January Tim Cook cut Apple's revenue forecast for the December quarter to about 84 billion dollars, below its earlier guidance, in a letter to investors. He blamed a much sharper slowdown in China than expected and fewer iPhone upgrades; sales outside the iPhone grew almost 19%.
why: The shares had already fallen about 30% from their peak in the autumn of 2018; the shift to services became the investment story.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000032019319000002/a8-kexhibit991122019.htm (Letter from Tim Cook to Apple investors, 2 January 2019, read 2026-10-03)

title: Two trillion dollars
what: On 19 August Apple's shares briefly topped 467 dollars, making it the first US company worth two trillion dollars, despite the pandemic. Apple has also announced that it will move its Macs from Intel processors to chips of its own design.
why: +21% in the month; Apple recovered quickly from the pandemic shock of early 2020. (Time check: in August 2020 the switch was announced, not yet under way.)

title: Profits fall in a weaker market
what: Apple reported an 11% fall in profit for the quarter to June compared with a year earlier, as technology shares have slid this year.
why: A pause after the pandemic boom; the shares fell about a quarter in 2022. (Time check: 'through 2022' assumed the rest of the year.)

title: The Vision Pro headset
what: At its developer conference Apple presented the Vision Pro, a headset that mixes the real world with digital images and is controlled by hand gestures, for 3,500 dollars.
why: Apple's first new product category since the Watch; it was considered a financial failure at first.

title: Apple Intelligence
what: At its developer conference Apple announced Apple Intelligence, artificial intelligence features for the iPhone, iPad and Mac, including the use of OpenAI's ChatGPT to improve Siri. Apple has been criticised for falling behind in AI. The shares rose and briefly made Apple the world's most valuable company again, ahead of Microsoft.
why: Apple's answer to the AI boom.

title: Tim Cook will hand over to John Ternus
what: On 20 April Apple announced that Tim Cook will become executive chair on 1 September and that John Ternus, 50, head of hardware engineering and at Apple since 2001, will succeed him as chief executive. On 30 April Apple reported record March-quarter revenue of 111.2 billion dollars, up 17%, with strong demand for the iPhone 17.
why: A planned succession after fifteen years of Cook, during which Apple's value rose more than tenfold.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000114036126015711/ef20071035_8k.htm (Apple 8-K of 20 April 2026, read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000032019326000011/a8-kex991q2202603282026.htm (Apple press release of 30 April 2026, read 2026-10-03)

title: John Ternus takes over
what: On 1 September John Ternus became Apple's chief executive, and Tim Cook executive chair.
why: The start of the post-Cook era; the shares are at a record.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000114036126035325/ef20081427_8ka.htm (Apple 8-K/A of 1 September 2026, read 2026-10-03, via EDGAR search listing); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Apple_Inc. (read 2026-10-03)
